title: Two-Layer Verification for Fault-Tolerant Magic-State Preparation in High-Rate Quantum Codes
abstract: Encoded magic states are essential for universal fault-tolerant quantum computation, but their resource-efficient preparation in high-rate quantum codes remains challenging. To address this limitation, we propose two-layer verification, which combines local verification of independently prepared subblocks with logical verification after their embedding into a target code. This hierarchy detects harmful error patterns, including even-parity logical-eigenvalue flips that are invisible to a collective product check alone. We demonstrate this scheme for a $[[21,3,5]]$ code by constructing a circuit that embeds three verified seven-qubit Steane-code magic states into the target code. Circuit-level simulations of $T$- and $S$-state preparation show logical-error suppression consistent with the code distance. These results demonstrate the potential of two-layer verification as a design principle for reliable magic-state preparation in quantum codes encoding multiple logical qubits.
summary: This paper proposes a two-layer verification scheme to overcome resource limitations in preparing magic states for fault-tolerant quantum computation. By combining local verification with a global product check, the method successfully mitigates systematic error patterns invisible to simpler checks. The results demonstrate that this approach achieves error suppression scaling comparable to established fault-tolerant codes.
main_problem: The challenge is to resource-efficiently prepare encoded magic states required for universal fault-tolerant quantum computation, especially within high-rate quantum codes.
main_result: The proposed two-layer verification scheme successfully suppresses logical errors, achieving a scaling consistent with fault-tolerant error correction for a distance-5 code.
method: The authors introduce a two-layer verification protocol: local verification of constituent subblocks followed by a global product-type logical verification after embedding into the target code.
model_or_system: The study focuses on the self-dual CSS $[[21, 3, 5]]$ quantum code. The process involves preparing and verifying three Steane-code magic states and embedding them into the larger target code.
key_observables: Logical error rate ($p_L$) and the scaling exponent ($\alpha$) relating $p_L$ to the physical error rate ($p_{	ext{circ}}$).
important_parameters: The code distance (d=5), the physical error rate ($p_{	ext{circ}}$), and the required number of physical qubits.
main_assumptions: The scheme assumes the target high-rate code supports a transversal implementation of the tensor product of the corresponding logical Clifford operators.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the two-layer verification overview, the decomposition of the encoder into subblocks, and numerical plots comparing the logical error rate scaling for different state preparation methods.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem, details the two-layer verification scheme (Layer 1: local checks; Layer 2: global checks), applies it to the $[[21, 3, 5]]$ code for T- and S-state preparation, and concludes with simulation results demonstrating error suppression.
why_interesting: The rigorous error analysis and the development of a structured verification protocol provide a blueprint for building reliable quantum computation primitives, which is fundamental to quantum information theory.

In the first layer, constituent encoded magic states, each corresponding to a logical qubit of the target high-rate code, are independently prepared and verified within separate subblocks. The accepted encoded states are rearranged by a SWAP network and embedded into the target code using a residual entangling circuit. In the second layer, product-type logical verification and fault-tolerant syndrome measurements for error detection are performed on the resulting encoded state. FIG. 2. Non-fault-tolerant arbitrary-state encoder for the [[21, 3, 5]] code. The three input states |ψj⟩are en- coded into the corresponding logical states. The circuit is obtained from a zero-state encoder by replacing three physi- cal |0⟩inputs with |ψj⟩and adding CNOT gates enclosed by the dashed rectangle. The additional CNOT gates are deter- mined by Gaussian elimination of the stabilizer and logical- operator matrices. At this stage, a single fault can propagate through CNOT gates to multiple physical qubits and produce harmful errors. Hence, the encoder is not fault tolerant.

FIG. 3. Decomposition of the arbitrary-state encoder. (A) The non-fault-tolerant encoder in Fig. 2 is decomposed into three Steane-code preparation subblocks, a SWAP network, and a residual entangling circuit. (B) First-layer verification for each Steane subblock, consisting of non-fault-tolerant encoding, flag-based physical-level logical verification, and Reichardt-type syndrome measurements [20]. (C) Detailed view of the SWAP network indicated by the box in (A). The physical qubits are appropriately rearranged before the residual entangling circuit is applied.

FIG. 6. Evaluation of logical outputs. (A) Evaluation of S-gate preparation with error-detecting teleportation (EDT). The logical S states prepared using the circuit in Fig. 5A, with error detection implemented by the noisy EDT circuit in Fig. 5B, are converted to logical |+⟩states by applying the inverse logical phase gate S−1 L , implemented by a transver- sal error-free physical S gate. Then, all physical qubits are ideally measured in the X basis. The measurement outcomes are decoded by the lookup-table decoder [19] dedicated to the [[21, 3, 5]] code. (A) The T-state injection box represents the circuit in Fig. 3A, which is followed by physical-level product-type logical verification and error detection.
